title: Punks, sex workers and society in transition: documenting postwar Japan – in pictures
text:
Punks, sex workers and society in transition: documenting postwar Japan – in pictures
A Long Shadow: Postwar Japan Through the Lens will be the first show of Japanese photography in more than three decades at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. The exhibit brings together 15 intergenerational artists as well as photographic prints, including more than 25 books and magazines and a video installation, all combining to show how photographers in Japan documented the country in the decades after the second world war. The exhibition runs until 2 May 2027
Ishikawa Mao, Red Flower: The Women of Okinawa, 1975–77. Photograph: Eugenia Burnett Tinsley/The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
‘We acquired a stunning print of this Tōmatsu Shōmei piece in 2023,’ says exhibition curator Lisa Sutcliffe. ‘It depicts a woman caught between blurred layers of chain-link fence at an American airbase in Okinawa. Fences were an important symbol for Tōmatsu, who described them as porous boundaries dividing rich and poor, past and present, east and west. His perspective was always from the outside looking in. For him, the perimeters of US military bases were particularly charged’Photograph: The Joyce F Menschel Photography Library, gift of Mary Ann and Frank B Arisman, in celebration of the Museum’s 150th Anniversary, 2020
‘Okinawa initially seemed like a compelling subject for an exhibition, bringing together questions of military occupation, sovereignty, rupture and identity,’ says Sutcliffe. ‘As my research developed, I expanded the scope to explore how photographers across Japan responded to and recorded the American military presence’Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Purchase, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, by exchange, 2026
Iida Takao, Non Vol 2: Okinawa Wa Nigayo (Okinawa is a Bitter World), 1970
‘The moment when Japanese artists turned to photography and publishing to make sense of the tremendous changes taking place around them feels relevant to the social transformations unfolding across the globe today. I think there is something instructive about looking at how artists of earlier generations responded to periods of uncertainty and upheaval, and what they hoped to communicate through their work. What might their experiences teach us about our own moment in history?’Photograph: The Joyce F Menschel Photography Library
Heshiki Kenshichi, Seeing the Customer Off, from the series Lungs of a Goat, 1970
‘Heshiki Kenshichi’s family owned a factory that supplied the American military with flak vests. His photographs like Seeing the Customer Off focus on the ordinary routines of this work. Rather than objectifying the women he photographed, Heshiki emphasizes their strength and agency. I find this image particularly evocative in the way it conveys the dignity, mystery and ritual of their work’Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
‘Over the past several decades, important exhibitions and publications have expanded our understanding of postwar Japanese photography, particularly the experimental work associated with the Provoke era’Photograph: Thomas J Watson Library, gift of Christopher Phillips, 2016
‘From Tōmatsu, who was responding to the historical moment in which he lived, to contemporary artists like Yamashiro Chikako, who continues to explore its consequences more than 50 years later, the exhibition reveals how the American military presence has shaped generations of artists in Japan and Okinawa. I hope visitors will consider the role of photography and art in shaping how history is constructed and remembered, and how its legacies continue to resonate in the present’Photograph: The Joyce F Menschel Photography Library
Ishiuchi Miyako (Japanese, b 1947), Yokosuka Story #5, from the series Yokosuka Story, 1977
‘Thanks to the pioneering scholarship of Kaneko Ryuichi, Toda Masako and Ivan Vartanian, photobooks have come to be recognized as works of art in their own right, and magazines are increasingly being studied as equally important sites of artistic experimentation. This has encouraged museums to think beyond individual prints and consider the many ways photographers conceived, sequenced and circulated their work’Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Purchase, Eileen Cohen Gift, Alfred Stieglitz Society Gifts, and Twentieth-Century Photography Fund, 2025
Ishikawa Mao, Red Flower: The Women of Okinawa, 1975–77
‘Ishikawa Mao’s intimate Red Flower series depicts women who worked as hostesses in bars frequented by Black American servicemen in Okinawa’Photograph: Eugenia Burnett Tinsley/The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
‘The Met had organized an exhibition of Tōmatsu’s work in 1992, and we were interested in building a stronger collection of his photographs and postwar Japanese photography more broadly’Photograph: Collection of David Dechman and Michel Mercure
‘Political and military histories often overlook the experiences of ordinary people whose lives are profoundly shaped by these events. These photographs offer the perspectives of artists, sex workers and islanders, revealing how the upheavals of the postwar period were experienced in everyday life, particularly by women whose stories are often left out of historical narratives’Photograph: Purchase, Eileen Cohen Gift, Alfred Stieglitz Society Gifts, and Twentieth Century Photography Fund, 2025
‘I hope visitors come away from this show with a more nuanced understanding of this period in Japanese and American history and the lasting impact of the American military occupation on Japanese society’Photograph: Alfred Stieglitz Society Gifts, 2025
